To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pore size distribution in a fabric stationary phase is described by a logistic function model and that cellulase enzymes decrease pore sizes uniformly.

the pore size distributions of cellulose fabrics are described by a simple logistic model and that enzyme treatment of fabrics decreases the pore sizes of the fabrics and decreases the retention of large molecules in size exclusion chromatography.

1) A simple logistic model captures the pore size distribution curve in a rolled stationary phase column; 2) The logistic model is useful in describing the effect of cellulase enzymes on pore size distribution; and 3) The logistic model enables comparison of pore sizes of untreated fabrics and enzyme‐treated fabrics in rolled stationary phases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model for pore size distribution of cellulose fabrics in rolled stationary phases.
the development of new stationary phases for liquid chromatography and their application to the rapid separation of protein and salt.
the development and characterization of a novel stationary phase that is a rolled fabric of regenerated cellulose fibers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the model of the pore size distribution in the rolled stationary phase columns was successfully obtained and that this model was able to describe the pore size distribution curves of the cellulose stationary phase.
a logistic model of pore size distribution is useful for modeling the separation of proteins and salts on rolled stationary phase columns.
the pore size distribution model for rolled stationary phases is a logistic function that can be used to predict the retention behavior of proteins and salts in these phases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pore size distribution curves are a useful tool to characterize and model the chromatography of rolled cellulose phases.
cellulose fabrics are not only suitable but ideal for size‐exclusion chromatography.
pore size distributions in rolled stationary phases can be modeled with a logistic function and the model is sensitive to cellulase treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the logistic function model is a useful way to describe the pore size distribution in cellulose rolled stationary phase columns.
the pore size distribution in cellulose stationary phases is well‐defined and can be used to predict the retention behavior of proteins and other molecules.
the fabric pore size distribution model can be used to predict how the chromatographic separation of proteins from salts will change when pore size distribution in the stationary phase is altered.
